why: The only coupling between rows is the total count x, and every value is positive, so the best you can take from row i is its limit[i] largest values. Pool those candidates and take the x largest: a top-k selection, not a DP, even though it sits in the 1-D DP week.
hints: Within one row, if you take j elements, which j should they be?
From row i only its top limit[i] values can ever be worth taking. Any x of the pooled candidates respects every row limit, so just take the x largest candidates.
Sort each row descending, pool its first limit[i] values, and sum the x largest (sort the pool or use a heap). If the pool has fewer than x values, return -1. O(n^2 log n).
pitfalls: Return -1 when the sum of limit[i] is less than x.
You must take exactly x, and the pool only contains up to limit[i] per row; don't take x from the whole matrix ignoring limits.
The sum can exceed 32 bits in other languages (up to 2500 * 10^4 here is fine, but return a long).
statement:
You are given an n x n integer matrix matrix, an array limit of length n, and an integer x.

Choose exactly x cells of the matrix so that, for every row i (0 <= i < n), at most limit[i] cells are chosen from row i. Return the largest possible sum of the chosen values, or -1 if exactly x cells cannot be chosen.

Worked example. limit = [1, 2, 1], matrix = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]], x = 2.

  • Best candidates per row: row 0 can give 3; row 1 can give 6, 5; row 2 can give 9.
  • Pool of candidates: 9, 6, 5, 3. Take the 2 largest: 9 (row 2) and 6 (row 1).
  • Answer: 15.
